newsitem.title: USA: Enron says would walk away from Portland.
newsitem.headline: Enron says would walk away from Portland.

text.p: Enron Corp is willing to walk away from its merger with Portland General Corp if it cannot secure a reasonable rate agreement with Oregon State, a spokesman for the company said.

"Portland General is a great company but if we do not think that this deal is in the best interest of Enron shareholders, we will not do it. There are plenty of other utilities," said a spokesman for Enron.

Portland General and Enron said on Thursday that the staff of the Oregon Public Utilities Commission was still demanding $141 million is savings for consumers against an offer of $61 million from the two companies.
Analysts were divided on whether a merger could be achieved.
Enron and Portland will now make presentations to the Commissioners of the Oregon Public Utilities Commission.
"We have finished our talks with the staff. There is no further negotiation with them," said the Enron spokesman.
However, he declined to comment on whether Enron and Portland were prepared to go some way to meeting the $141 million in cost savings.
"I simply cannot comment on that. That is our offer, we will just have to see what they say," he said.
Analysts were divided on whether a deal could be made.

"We believe that the deal will go ahead and that the companies and the staff of the commission will come to an arrangement that is in the interest of the companies and the consumer," said Ron Barone, analyst at PaineWebber.
Portland slid 0-7/8 to 36-1/4 by 0955 EST and Enron gained 3/8 at 39-1/2.
Some analysts said that Portland may now be back in play and suggested that other potential partners include KN Energy, Questar, Consolidated Natural Gas or El Paso Natural Gas.
"The company may now be tempted to go for an alliance or joint venture," said Susan Weaver, analyst at Howard Weil.
"The Oregon PUC appears to have said that Enron is going to come in and make so much money off this that they should have a lot of savings for their customers and they may not budge," she added.
The merger had already been approved by the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC).
"The state is bound to be much more political than the FERC," said one analyst, who declined to be named.
Enron plans to turn itself into the largest electricity wholesaler in the country, overtaking Southern Co, chief executive Kenneth Lay told PaineWebber's energy conference in New York last month.
Analysts say these plans may have been dented short-term, but Enron is an aggressive player.

"It is negative for Enron short-term but I am sure they have a list of alternatives. I do not think they are going to abandon this strategy, they are the leader in this industry," said Howard Weil's Weaver.
((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
